_meta.description: Curated reference list of commonly discussed substances/conditions across diet, personal care, and environment. Educational/awareness use only. concern_level is a coarse 1-3 heuristic reflecting how consistently a substance is flagged as worth-managing in public-health/regulatory guidance, NOT a clinical or regulatory risk rating, and it does NOT account for dose — the amount in a typical consumer product or serving is almost always far below levels studied in the underlying research. pubchem_name/pubmed_query drive sources/sync_db.py, which fetches live GHS hazard data and real peer-reviewed citations (see references[] and regulatory{} after a sync run, and last_synced for when).

substances.name: Parabens
substances.summary: Preservatives used in cosmetics/personal care products; weak estrogen-mimicking activity reported in lab studies. Widely used and considered low-risk by regulators at typical use levels, but frequently flagged by consumers seeking to minimize endocrine-disrupting-chemical (EDC) exposure.
mitigation_tips: Look for 'paraben-free' labeling if limiting hormone-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) is a priority.
Rotate/diversify personal care brands rather than using one product exclusively long-term.

substances.technical_note: Parabens are rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases in skin and liver to para-hydroxybenzoic acid, then conjugated and excreted in urine within hours — they do not meaningfully bioaccumulate. Their estrogen-receptor binding is several orders of magnitude weaker than estradiol; the more relevant concern is aggregate exposure across the many products a person uses in one day, not any single application.
substances.summary_plain: Preservatives that keep cosmetics from spoiling. In lab studies they act a little like the hormone estrogen. Regulators say the amounts normally used are not a concern, but some people choose to limit them.

substances.name: Phthalates
substances.summary: Often hidden inside generic 'fragrance/parfum' listings; used as plasticizers and fragrance carriers. Associated in research with endocrine disruption; classified with higher concern by several advocacy and regulatory bodies compared to parabens.
mitigation_tips: Choose 'fragrance-free' (not just 'unscented') products, since unscented can still use masking fragrance.
Ventilate bathrooms well when using fragranced products.

substances.technical_note: Phthalates are rapidly metabolized (hepatic hydrolysis to monoester metabolites, then glucuronidation) and cleared renally with urinary half-lives of hours — which is why biomonitoring studies use spot urine samples: they reflect very recent exposure, not a stored body burden. Because clearance is fast, same-day aggregate exposure (fragrance across several products at once) matters more than any one product in isolation.
substances.summary_plain: Chemicals that make plastic flexible and help scent last. They can hide behind the word 'fragrance' on a label. Research links some of them to effects on hormones, and several groups rate them a higher concern than parabens.

substances.name: Sodium Lauryl Sulfate (SLS) / Sodium Laureth Sulfate (SLES)
substances.summary: Common surfactants/foaming agents. Primarily associated with skin/eye irritation and stripping natural oils, especially with frequent use or on sensitive skin, rather than systemic toxicity concerns. SLES manufacturing can leave trace 1,4-dioxane contamination.
mitigation_tips: If experiencing scalp/skin irritation or dryness, try sulfate-free formulations.
Reduce wash frequency or dilute product if irritation is noted.

substances.summary_plain: Foaming cleansers found in shampoo and soap. They mostly irritate the skin or eyes and can dry the skin, especially with frequent use or on sensitive skin. They are not mainly a whole-body concern. SLES can carry traces of 1,4-dioxane from how it is made.

substances.name: Formaldehyde-releasing preservatives
substances.summary: Preservatives that slowly release small amounts of formaldehyde (a known human carcinogen at high/occupational exposure) to inhibit microbial growth. Can trigger contact dermatitis in sensitized individuals.
mitigation_tips: If you have known formaldehyde sensitivity or contact dermatitis, patch test new products and check ingredient lists.
Consider preservative systems like sodium benzoate/potassium sorbate as an alternative.

substances.technical_note: Released formaldehyde is rapidly oxidized by alcohol/aldehyde dehydrogenase (the same enzyme family that metabolizes ingested alcohol) to formate, then further processed or excreted — it does not accumulate. The consumer-product concern is primarily localized contact sensitization in already-sensitized skin, mechanistically distinct from the much higher-dose inhalation cancer data (occupational settings) behind its GHS carcinogen classification.
substances.summary_plain: Preservatives that slowly give off tiny amounts of formaldehyde to stop germs growing. At high, workplace-level exposure, formaldehyde is known to cause cancer. In people who have become sensitive to them, these preservatives can cause a skin rash.

substances.name: Artificial food dyes
substances.summary: Synthetic colorants used in cereals, pastries, and drinks. Some studies link certain dyes to hyperactivity in sensitive children; regulatory status varies by country (several require warning labels in the EU, and the U.S. FDA revoked authorization for Red Dye 3 in food in 2025).
mitigation_tips: Choose whole-food breakfast options (oats, fruit, eggs) over brightly-colored processed cereals.
Check labels on kids' breakfast products specifically, where dye use is concentrated.
substances.pubmed_query: synthetic food dyes children behavior hyperactivity

references.title: Synthetic Colors in Food: A Warning for Children's Health
references.journal: Int J Environ Res Public Health

The influence of components of diet on the symptoms of ADHD in children

ghs_hazards: Not Classified

substances.technical_note: Most approved synthetic dyes are poorly absorbed from the gut and largely excreted unchanged in feces. The hyperactivity research concern is a proposed direct neurobehavioral effect in sensitive children — mechanistically different from most other entries here, which center on absorption/metabolism/accumulation.
substances.summary_plain: Man-made colors used in cereal, pastries and drinks. Some studies link certain dyes to hyperactivity in sensitive children. Rules differ by country: the EU puts warning labels on some, and in 2025 the US FDA withdrew its approval of Red Dye 3 in food.

substances.name: Added/refined sugar
substances.summary: Not a 'toxin' in the classic sense: what matters is how much and how often. A 2023 umbrella review of 73 meta-analyses (BMJ) found high sugar intake, especially from sugar-sweetened drinks, linked to poorer cardiometabolic outcomes, though most of the evidence was rated low quality; its authors suggest keeping added sugars under about 25 g a day.
mitigation_tips: Pair carbohydrates with protein/fiber at breakfast to blunt glucose spikes.
Swap sweetened cereal/yogurt for plain versions with fresh fruit.
substances.pubmed_query: added sugar intake metabolic health outcomes

references.title: Dietary sugar consumption and health: umbrella review

Consumption of sugar sweetened beverages, artificially sweetened beverages, and fruit juice and incidence of type 2 diabetes: systematic review, meta-analysis, and estimation of population attributable fraction
Sugar-Sweetened Beverages and Adverse Human Health Outcomes: An Umbrella Review of Meta-Analyses of Observational Studies

substances.technical_note: This isn't a xenobiotic clearance question at all — glucose and fructose enter normal carbohydrate metabolism. The concern is purely dose and frequency (glycemic load, hepatic fructose handling at high chronic intake), which is part of why it carries the lowest concern level in this database despite being ubiquitous.
substances.summary_plain: Sugar is not a poison. What matters is how much and how often. A large 2023 review in the BMJ linked a lot of sugar, especially from sweet drinks, to poorer heart and metabolic health, though most of the evidence was low quality. Its authors suggest keeping added sugar under about 25 grams a day.

substances.name: Acrylamide
substances.summary: Forms naturally in starchy foods during high-heat cooking (toasting, frying, baking) via the Maillard/browning reaction. Classified as a probable human carcinogen based on animal studies at high doses; dietary exposure levels are much lower.
mitigation_tips: Toast bread to golden rather than dark brown/black.
Vary starch sources (e.g., some mornings oats or eggs instead of toast/hash browns).

substances.summary_plain: Forms naturally in starchy foods when they are toasted, fried or baked at high heat and turn brown. It is a probable cancer-causing substance, based on animal studies at high doses. The amounts people eat are much lower.

substances.name: BPA (Bisphenol A)
substances.summary: Used in some plastic containers and can linings; an endocrine-disrupting chemical that can migrate into food/drink, especially with heat.
mitigation_tips: Avoid microwaving food in plastic containers.
Prefer glass/stainless storage for reheated breakfast leftovers.

Its estrogen-receptor activity is weak relative to estradiol; the more actively debated science concerns low-dose, non-monotonic effects rather than accumulation.
substances.summary_plain: Used in some hard plastics and in the lining of some cans. It acts on hormones, and it can move into food and drink, especially when heated.

substances.name: Titanium dioxide (food-grade, E171)
substances.summary: A whitening/opacifying additive used in some candies, coffee creamers, and frostings. The European Food Safety Authority withdrew its 'safe' determination in 2021 citing inability to rule out genotoxicity concerns from nanoparticle-sized fractions, and the EU banned it as a food additive in 2022; the U.S. FDA still permits it.
mitigation_tips: Check labels on creamers/candies for 'titanium dioxide' or 'E171' if minimizing intake.
Whole-milk or plant-milk creamers typically don't need it.

substances.summary_plain: A whitener added to some candy, creamers and frosting. In 2021 European food-safety experts withdrew their finding that it is safe, because they could not rule out DNA damage from its very tiny particles. The EU banned it in food in 2022. The US FDA still allows it.

substances.name: Sodium nitrite (cured meat preservative)
substances.summary: Used to cure bacon, sausage, and deli meat; can form nitrosamines (probable carcinogens) when heated at high temperatures, particularly alongside protein. IARC classifies processed meat as a Group 1 (carcinogenic) exposure, with nitrite chemistry as one proposed mechanism.
mitigation_tips: Pair cured breakfast meats with vitamin-C-rich foods (citrus, peppers), which can inhibit nitrosamine formation.
Cook bacon/sausage at moderate heat rather than charring, and swap in eggs/plant protein some mornings.

This is mechanistically why the vitamin-C mitigation tip works: ascorbate competes for the nitrosation reaction itself, blocking formation before metabolism is even relevant.
substances.summary_plain: Used to cure bacon, sausage and deli meat. When heated to high temperatures, especially with protein, it can form nitrosamines, which are probable cancer-causing substances. The cancer agency IARC puts processed meat in Group 1, which describes how strong the evidence is, not how big the effect is. Nitrite is one proposed reason.

substances.name: BHA / BHT (synthetic antioxidant preservatives)
substances.summary: Synthetic antioxidants that prevent fats from going rancid in cereals, snack bars, and packaged baked goods. BHA is listed by the U.S. National Toxicology Program as 'reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen' based on animal data; BHT evidence is more mixed.
mitigation_tips: Look for cereals/snack bars preserved with vitamin E (tocopherols) instead of BHA/BHT.
Buying nuts/oats in smaller quantities and refrigerating reduces the need for synthetic antioxidant preservation at home.

substances.name: PFAS ("forever chemicals") in food packaging
substances.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances used to make packaging grease/water resistant (fast-food wrappers, some microwave popcorn bags, takeout containers) and some non-stick cookware coatings. Extremely persistent in the body and environment; associated in research with a range of health effects. As older "long-chain" PFAS like PFOA were phased out, manufacturers largely moved to "short-chain" replacements (e.g. GenX) marketed as safer because they clear the body faster -- but the U.S. FDA and several states have moved to phase out PFAS broadly in food packaging as of the mid-2020s, not just the older compounds.
mitigation_tips: Transfer takeout/fast food to a plate rather than eating directly from grease-resistant wrapping when practical.
Retire non-stick pans once the coating is visibly scratched or worn.
Air-pop popcorn or use a stovetop method instead of microwave bags occasionally.

substances.technical_note: This is the one entry where the usual 'liver/kidneys handle it in hours' story doesn't apply: PFAS's charged head group is actively reabsorbed by renal organic anion transporters instead of being excreted, giving serum half-lives measured in years rather than hours for the older long-chain compounds. Short-chain replacements like GenX (HFPO-DA) do clear faster -- but a 2020 NIEHS/EPA study dosing pregnant mice with PFOA or GenX side by side found GenX reproduced many of PFOA's maternal and developmental effects regardless of that shorter half-life, i.e. faster clearance didn't translate to a cleanly better safety profile. That's the general shape of 'regrettable substitution': a replacement engineered to fix one specific, measurable property (persistence) without the underlying toxicity necessarily following.
substances.summary_plain: 'Forever chemicals' that make packaging resist grease and water: fast-food wrappers, some microwave popcorn bags, takeout boxes and some non-stick pans. They last a very long time in the body and the environment, and research links them to a range of health effects. The US FDA and several states are phasing out PFAS in food packaging, including newer 'short-chain' types like GenX.

substances.name: Indoor mold / mycotoxin exposure
substances.summary: Indoor mold growth (often from past water damage, humidity, or poor ventilation) can trigger respiratory symptoms, allergic reactions, and in some individuals broader symptom clusters attributed to mycotoxin exposure. Home and workplace HVAC systems are common reservoirs.
mitigation_tips: Run bathroom exhaust fans during/after showers; fix leaks promptly.
Have HVAC systems and ductwork inspected/cleaned if musty odors are present.
Consider a hygrometer to keep indoor humidity under ~50%.
For confirmed mold or persistent symptoms, consult a certified mold inspector and a physician rather than self-diagnosing.
substances.pubmed_query: indoor dampness mold respiratory health review

references.title: Respiratory and allergic health effects of dampness, mold, and dampness-related agents: a review of the epidemiologic evidence
Indoor fungal exposure
Does dampness and mold in schools affect health? Results of a meta-analysis

substances.technical_note: For most people, symptoms are IgE-mediated allergic responses to inhaled spore/hyphal fragments (subject to the same size-dependent deposition physics as other airborne particles), not mycotoxin poisoning. True mycotoxicosis requires much higher, sustained exposure than typical household contact and is a distinct, much rarer clinical picture from the common allergic/irritant presentation.
substances.summary_plain: Mold can grow indoors after water damage, damp air or poor airflow. It can cause breathing problems and allergic reactions. In some people it is blamed for a wider mix of symptoms, linked to substances some molds make (mycotoxins). Heating and cooling systems are common places for it to hide.

substances.name: Stale/overdue HVAC filter
substances.summary: Overdue HVAC filters recirculate dust, particulates, and can harbor microbial growth, contributing to indoor air quality (IAQ) degradation.
mitigation_tips: Replace/check filters roughly every 1-3 months (more often with pets or allergies).
Request workplace facilities confirm HVAC filter maintenance schedules.
substances.pubmed_query: HVAC filter maintenance indoor air quality health

references.title: In-situ effectiveness of residential HVAC filters
In situ efficiency of filters in residential central HVAC systems
Evaluating the Long-Term Health and Economic Impacts of Central Residential Air Filtration for Reducing Premature Mortality Associated with Indoor Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) of Outdoor Origin
references.journal: Int J Environ Res Public Health

substances.technical_note: A filter's MERV rating describes what particle size it captures efficiently. An overdue filter doesn't just stop filtering well — the pressure drop across a clogged filter can reduce total airflow, which paradoxically cuts total air changes per hour along with filtration efficiency.
substances.summary_plain: A clogged or overdue air filter sends dust and tiny particles around the home, and can let germs and mold grow. That makes indoor air worse.

substances.name: VOC off-gassing
substances.summary: Volatile organic compounds off-gas from paints, new furniture, carpet, and some cleaning/air-freshening products, contributing to indoor air pollution and, in some individuals, headaches or respiratory irritation.
mitigation_tips: Ventilate spaces well after painting or installing new furniture/carpet (days to weeks).
Choose low-VOC paints/products where possible.
Use a portable air purifier with activated carbon for VOC adsorption in problem rooms.
substances.pubmed_query: volatile organic compounds indoor air quality health effects

references.title: Indoor Air Pollution and the Health of Vulnerable Groups: A Systematic Review Focused on Particulate Matter (PM), Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) and Their Effects on Children and People with Pre-Existing Lung Disease

substances.technical_note: VOC off-gassing follows roughly first-order decay from a fresh material — highest emission immediately after installation/application, dropping over days to weeks. That's the physical reason 'ventilate for the first couple weeks' is the standard advice rather than an indefinite precaution.
substances.summary_plain: New paint, furniture and carpet, and some cleaning and air-freshening products, give off gases called VOCs. They add to indoor air pollution. In some people they cause headaches or an irritated nose and throat.

substances.name: Low indoor humidity
substances.summary: Very low indoor humidity (common in AC-heavy or heated environments) can dry mucous membranes, reducing natural defenses against airborne irritants and pathogens.
mitigation_tips: Consider a humidifier for very dry environments (target ~30-50% relative humidity).
Stay hydrated and use saline nasal spray if mucous membranes feel dry.
substances.pubmed_query: low indoor humidity respiratory infection risk

references.title: Indoor air humidity, air quality, and health - An overview

Relative Humidity and Its Impact on the Immune System and Infections

substances.technical_note: Low humidity doesn't introduce a new chemical exposure — the mechanism is desiccation of the nasal/respiratory mucociliary barrier, the body's primary first-line particle/pathogen clearance system. This entry is more 'reduced defense' than 'exposure' in the sense the rest of this database uses.
substances.summary_plain: Very dry indoor air, common with heating or air conditioning, can dry out the lining of your nose and throat. That makes it easier for irritants and germs in the air to get past your natural defenses.

substances.name: High indoor humidity
substances.summary: Sustained high indoor humidity (>60%) promotes dust mite and mold growth, compounding respiratory exposure risks.
mitigation_tips: Use dehumidifiers in consistently damp areas.
Improve ventilation (exhaust fans, cracked windows) in high-moisture rooms.
substances.pubmed_query: indoor humidity dust mite allergen asthma

references.title: Indirect health effects of relative humidity in indoor environments
Dehumidifiers for chronic asthma
Humidity regulation in the management of asthma patients sensitized to house dust mites

substances.technical_note: Above roughly 60% relative humidity, dust mite and mold growth rates increase sharply — this entry is really an upstream risk factor feeding the `mold_indoor` and dust-mite-allergen pathways rather than an exposure in its own right.
substances.summary_plain: Air that stays humid, over about 60%, helps dust mites and mold grow. That adds to what you breathe in.

substances.name: Cyclic siloxanes (D4/D5)
substances.summary: Silicone-derived ingredients that give hair/skin products a smooth, silky feel. D4 is classified by the EU as a substance of very high concern (endocrine disruption, environmental persistence) and is restricted there; D5 is more debated. Most dimethicone itself (the polymer) is considered lower concern than the cyclic (ring-shaped) siloxane monomers D4/D5.
mitigation_tips: If minimizing siloxane exposure, scan ingredient lists for 'cyclopentasiloxane' or 'cyclotetrasiloxane' specifically (not just any 'dimethicone').
Rinse-off products (shampoo/conditioner) carry lower systemic exposure than leave-on products.

substances.name: Aluminum compounds (antiperspirant)
substances.summary: Aluminum salts block sweat ducts in antiperspirants. A commonly raised link to breast cancer has not been supported by the larger body of epidemiological evidence to date, though research is ongoing; skin irritation is the more established concern, especially on freshly shaved skin.
mitigation_tips: If irritation occurs, apply after shaving has fully settled (few hours) rather than immediately.
Aluminum-free deodorants (which control odor but not sweat) are a straightforward alternative if you'd prefer to avoid aluminum salts.

substances.technical_note: Only a small fraction of topically applied aluminum salts penetrates intact skin; what's absorbed is renally cleared like other aluminum compounds. Most people's larger absorbed dose is actually dietary (aluminum-containing food additives, cookware, antacids), part of why epidemiological evidence hasn't supported antiperspirant use specifically as a meaningful driver of health outcomes.
substances.summary_plain: Aluminum salts block sweat glands in antiperspirants. People often raise a link to breast cancer, but the larger body of research has not supported it so far, and studies continue. Skin irritation is the better-established concern, especially on freshly shaved skin.

substances.name: Talc
substances.summary: A mineral used as a powder base in some cosmetic and body powders. Historical concern centers on possible contamination with asbestos (a known carcinogen) from shared mineral deposits; asbestos-free talc's own cancer risk (e.g., from perineal use) has been debated in epidemiological studies with mixed results.
mitigation_tips: Cornstarch-based powders are a widely available talc-free alternative.
Look for products that state third-party asbestos testing if continuing to use talc-based powder.

The old worry was contamination with asbestos, a known cancer-causing substance, found in some of the same deposits. Studies on whether talc without asbestos can cause cancer, for example with genital use, have had mixed results.

substances.name: Retinyl palmitate (in daytime sunscreen)
substances.summary: A vitamin A derivative added to some sunscreens/moisturizers as an antioxidant/anti-aging ingredient. A U.S. NTP photocarcinogenicity study in mice raised a question about accelerated skin tumor development under intense UV exposure specifically when combined with UV light; the finding hasn't been confirmed in humans and regulators have not restricted its use, but it's part of why some sunscreen guides suggest checking for it in daily-wear, sun-exposed products.
mitigation_tips: Mineral sunscreens (zinc oxide / titanium dioxide based) are a straightforward alternative if avoiding retinyl palmitate specifically.
This is unrelated to topical retinoids used at night for skin care, which is a separate use case with different evidence.

substances.name: Triclosan
substances.summary: An antibacterial agent formerly common in liquid hand soap. The U.S. FDA banned triclosan (and 18 other antibacterial ingredients) from over-the-counter wash products in 2016/2017 citing insufficient evidence that it's more effective than plain soap plus emerging safety questions (endocrine activity, antibiotic resistance concerns); it can still appear in some toothpaste and cosmetics.
mitigation_tips: Plain soap and water is equally effective for routine handwashing per FDA's own rationale for the ban.
Check toothpaste ingredient lists if you specifically want to avoid it; it's less common than it used to be.

There was not enough evidence that it works better than plain soap, and there were questions about hormone effects and antibiotic resistance. It can still turn up in some toothpaste and cosmetics.

substances.name: Radon gas
substances.summary: A naturally occurring radioactive gas that seeps from soil/rock into homes, especially basements. It's the second-leading cause of lung cancer in the U.S. after smoking per the EPA/Surgeon General, and is completely undetectable without testing (no smell, no visible sign).
mitigation_tips: Test your home with an inexpensive radon test kit (short-term kits are ~$15-25) — the EPA recommends every home be tested.
If levels are at/above 4 pCi/L, a radon mitigation system (sub-slab depressurization) reliably brings levels down and typically costs a low-to-mid four-figure sum.
Retest after any major renovation or if you move into a new home.

substances.technical_note: See the alpha-radiation concept above — radon's decay products deposit in the bronchial epithelium and emit short-range, high-energy alpha radiation there, which is mechanistically why inhalation (not ingestion, e.g. from well water) dominates its lung cancer risk, and why it's a fundamentally different hazard type than any chemical entry in this database.
substances.summary_plain: A natural radioactive gas that seeps up from soil and rock into homes, especially basements. After smoking, it is the second leading cause of lung cancer in the US, according to the EPA and the Surgeon General. You cannot see or smell it, so the only way to know is to test.

substances.name: Lead (older homes/plumbing)
substances.summary: Homes built before 1978 (U.S.) may have lead-based paint; some older plumbing/service lines still contain lead. No safe blood lead level has been identified, particularly for children's neurodevelopment; adults are also affected at high exposure.
mitigation_tips: If your home was built before 1978, get paint tested before sanding/renovating, or hire an EPA Lead-Safe Certified contractor.
Run cold tap water for 30-60 seconds before drinking/cooking if you have older plumbing, especially after the tap has sat unused for hours.
A home water test or an inexpensive filter certified for lead removal (NSF/ANSI 53) addresses the plumbing pathway specifically.

That's why past exposure can matter years later, and why 'no safe level' is the standard public-health framing rather than a dose threshold.
substances.summary_plain: Homes built before 1978 in the US may have lead paint, and some older water pipes still contain lead. No safe blood lead level has been found, especially for children's developing brains. Adults are affected too at high exposure.

substances.name: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5)
substances.summary: Airborne particles ≤2.5 microns wide (from traffic, wildfire smoke, cooking, industrial sources) that penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream. Associated with cardiovascular and respiratory effects; the EPA tightened the annual PM2.5 air quality standard in 2024. Log a reading (from a local monitor, an app like AirNow, or a personal sensor) under Journey › Air to have it scored automatically by AQI category.
mitigation_tips: On high-PM2.5 days (check airnow.gov or a local app), keep windows closed and run a HEPA air purifier if available.
Use exhaust ventilation (range hood) when cooking, especially with a gas stove.
An N95/KN95 mask reduces personal exposure during outdoor smoke events.

references.title: Air pollution and children's health-a review of adverse effects associated with prenatal exposure from fine to ultrafine particulate matter

substances.technical_note: See the particle-deposition concept above — PM2.5's alveolar penetration is precisely why it's treated as higher-concern than PM10 despite PM10 being the more 'visible' pollutant; alveolar-deposited particles are also positioned to cross into systemic circulation more readily than particles cleared by the upper-airway mucociliary escalator.
substances.summary_plain: Tiny particles in the air, 2.5 microns wide or smaller, from traffic, wildfire smoke, cooking and industry. They reach deep into the lungs and the bloodstream, and are linked to heart and lung effects. The EPA tightened its yearly PM2.5 standard in 2024. You can log a reading from a local monitor, the AirNow app or your own sensor under Journey, then Air.

substances.name: Chlorination byproducts (THMs) in tap water
substances.summary: Trihalomethanes form when chlorine disinfectant reacts with organic matter in municipal water treatment. Regulated by the EPA under the Safe Drinking Water Act; levels in U.S. municipal water are generally kept below the regulatory limit, though some systems have had periodic exceedances, and long-term high exposure has been studied for a possible modest bladder cancer association.
mitigation_tips: Check your local water utility's annual Consumer Confidence Report (public, usually online) for your system's THM (trihalomethane) levels.
An activated-carbon filter (pitcher or faucet-mount, NSF/ANSI 53 certified) reduces THMs in drinking water if levels are a concern.
This is a minor, well-regulated exposure for most U.S. municipal water — not a reason to avoid tap water by default.

substances.name: Nitrogen dioxide (gas stove combustion)
substances.summary: Gas and propane stoves release nitrogen dioxide and other combustion byproducts during use, especially without ventilation. Indoor NO2 levels in homes with gas stoves and no range hood use can exceed outdoor air quality standards; associated with respiratory irritation and, in children, increased asthma risk.
mitigation_tips: Run the range hood (vented to the outside, not recirculating) every time you use a gas burner or oven — this is the single highest-leverage change.
Crack a window when cooking on gas if you don't have a vented hood.
If replacing a stove, induction ranges eliminate combustion byproducts entirely.

substances.summary_plain: Gas and propane stoves give off nitrogen dioxide and other gases from burning, especially without ventilation. In homes with a gas stove and no range hood use, indoor levels can go above outdoor air standards. It is linked to airway irritation and, in children, a higher chance of asthma.

substances.name: Candle and incense smoke (indoor PM2.5)
substances.summary: Burning candles and incense releases fine particulate matter and, for heavily fragranced candles, some of the same VOCs found in air fresheners. Occasional use is a minor contributor; daily heavy use in a small, unventilated room adds up similarly to other indoor PM2.5 sources.
mitigation_tips: Crack a window or run an exhaust fan when burning candles/incense for extended periods.
Trim wicks and avoid letting candles smoke visibly — visible soot means more particulate output.
Reserve daily ambiance for flameless (LED) candles or a diffuser using a few drops of essential oil in water instead.

substances.summary_plain: Burning candles and incense releases fine particles. Heavily scented candles can also release some of the same VOC gases as air fresheners. Now and then is a small contribution. Daily heavy use in a small, closed room adds up much like other indoor sources of fine particles.

substances.name: Microplastics (bottled water & reheated plastic)
substances.summary: Bottled water and food reheated in plastic can shed microscopic plastic particles, especially with heat or repeated reuse of thin single-use bottles. Health effects of microplastic ingestion at typical dietary levels are still an active, unsettled area of research — concern here is precautionary rather than based on established harm.
mitigation_tips: A reusable stainless steel or glass water bottle with filtered tap water sidesteps this entirely and is also cheaper long-term.
Never microwave food in plastic containers, even ones labeled 'microwave-safe' for leaks — that label covers structural safety, not particle shedding.

substances.technical_note: The open toxicological question here is genuinely about fate, not just presence: what fraction of ingested microplastic particles cross the gut epithelium versus pass through unabsorbed is still an active research area — exactly why this entry carries the lowest concern level in the database despite the exposure route itself being well-documented.
substances.summary_plain: Bottled water, and food reheated in plastic, can shed tiny plastic particles, especially with heat or when thin single-use bottles are reused. What these particles do to health at everyday amounts is still being studied. The concern here is a precaution, not a proven harm.

substances.name: Dry-cleaning solvent residue (PERC)
substances.summary: Perchloroethylene (PERC), the most common dry-cleaning solvent, off-gasses from freshly dry-cleaned garments stored in a closed closet or worn soon after pickup. Occupational exposure (dry-cleaning workers) is the better-established concern; residue on finished garments in home use is a much smaller, precautionary-level exposure.
mitigation_tips: Remove the plastic garment bag and air out dry-cleaned items outside or in a well-ventilated room for a few hours to a day before wearing or storing them in a closet.
Ask if your cleaner offers 'wet cleaning' or liquid CO2 cleaning — both are PERC-free alternatives now offered by many cleaners.

substances.name: Lawn/garden pesticide residue tracked indoors
substances.summary: Pesticides and herbicides applied to lawns don't stay outside — studies of household dust and carpet consistently find them tracked indoors on shoes and pet paws, where they persist far longer than outdoors (out of UV light and rain). This is one of the more overlooked indoor exposure pathways precisely because the application itself happens outside.
mitigation_tips: A shoes-off-at-the-door household habit is the single most effective, lowest-cost intervention for this entire pathway (also reduces lead dust, pollen, and general dirt).
Wipe pet paws after they've been on treated grass.
If you hire a lawn service, ask for the product name and keep kids/pets off treated areas for the reentry interval printed on the product label.

substances.name: Household dust (chemical reservoir)
substances.summary: House dust isn't just dirt — it's a well-studied reservoir that accumulates flame retardants (from furniture/electronics), lead (from old paint), pesticides, and phthalates that have settled out of the air or worn off products over time. Regular dust removal is one of the few interventions that reduces exposure to several unrelated substance families at once.
mitigation_tips: Vacuum with a HEPA-filter vacuum weekly, focusing on carpet and upholstery.
Wet-mop or wet-wipe hard floors and surfaces rather than dry-dusting, which just resuspends particles into the air.
Wash hands before eating, especially for kids who play on the floor — hand-to-mouth contact is the main route dust exposure actually reaches the body.

That's why dust removal is one of the few single interventions touching multiple substance families in this database at once.
substances.summary_plain: House dust is more than dirt. It builds up flame retardants from furniture and electronics, lead from old paint, pesticides, and phthalates that have settled out of the air or worn off products. Regular dusting and cleaning is one of the few steps that lowers exposure to several unrelated chemical groups at once.

substances.name: Overheated nonstick cookware (PTFE)
substances.summary: PTFE nonstick coatings are considered stable at normal cooking temperatures, but overheating an empty or near-empty nonstick pan (above ~500°F/260°C) can release fumes that are acutely toxic to birds and cause temporary flu-like symptoms in people ('polymer fume fever'). Scratched/worn coatings are the other main concern, both for fume release and ingesting flaked coating.
mitigation_tips: Never preheat a nonstick pan empty on high heat — add oil or food first, and keep to medium heat or below.
Use kitchen ventilation (range hood) when cooking, which helps with this and the separate gas-stove NO2 issue.
Retire a nonstick pan once the coating is visibly scratched, flaking, or peeling; cast iron or stainless steel are scratch-proof alternatives for high-heat cooking.

substances.technical_note: Intact PTFE is chemically and thermally stable at normal cooking temperatures — it isn't absorbed or metabolized. The fume-fever mechanism is acute inhalation of pyrolysis breakdown products released only above roughly 260°C (500°F), a threshold an empty pan on high heat reaches well before typical cooking temperatures with food or oil in the pan.
substances.summary_plain: Nonstick coatings (PTFE) are stable at normal cooking temperatures. An empty pan heated above about 500°F (260°C) can give off fumes that harm pet birds and can cause a short flu-like illness in people. Scratched or worn coatings are the other main concern.

substances.name: Fragranced laundry products (detergent, dryer sheets)
substances.summary: Scented detergents, fabric softeners, and dryer sheets release VOCs during the wash/dry cycle (often vented straight outside from the dryer, but also lingering on fabric and in the laundry room) and leave a fragrance residue on clothing and bedding worn/used against skin for hours at a time.
mitigation_tips: Fragrance-free detergent is widely available at the same price point and gets clothes equally clean — this is a zero-cost swap.
Wool dryer balls are a fragrance-free alternative to dryer sheets for reducing static.
Ventilate the laundry room, especially if the dryer vents indoors (uncommon but worth checking).

substances.technical_note: This entry sits at the intersection of two pathways: inhaled VOCs off-gassing from the wash/dry cycle, and direct dermal contact from residue on fabric worn for hours — which is part of why it's tagged low concern individually but still contributes to a household's aggregate fragrance-chemical exposure alongside personal care products.
substances.summary_plain: Scented detergent, fabric softener and dryer sheets release VOC gases while you wash and dry. Much of it is vented outside from the dryer, but some lingers on fabric and in the laundry room. The scent also stays on clothes and bedding that touch your skin for hours.

substances.name: Bisphenol analogs (BPS, BPF, BPAF)
substances.summary: Close chemical relatives of BPA, commonly swapped in to make a product 'BPA-free' -- same can-lining/plastic/thermal-receipt-paper uses, same general molecular shape. Research directly comparing them to BPA has found similar hormonal activity, not a safety improvement, which is why toxicologists call this pattern 'regrettable substitution.'
mitigation_tips: A 'BPA-free' label describes what's absent, not what replaced it -- the same avoid-heat-and-reheating habits that reduce BPA exposure apply here too.
Glass, stainless, or ceramic sidesteps the whole bisphenol family, not just BPA specifically.
substances.pubmed_query: bisphenol S bisphenol F endocrine activity BPA substitute
substances.technical_note: BPS and BPF share BPA's diphenylmethane-derived backbone and its weak estrogen-receptor affinity; a 2015 systematic review (Rochester & Bolden, Environmental Health Perspectives) pooling 32 studies found their hormonal potency in the same order of magnitude as BPA, acting through the same estrogenic, antiestrogenic, androgenic, and antiandrogenic pathways. Chemical safety testing has historically evaluated compounds one at a time rather than by structural family, which is part of why a like-for-like replacement can clear a 'BPA-free' bar without the underlying biological activity actually changing.

substances.name: Phenoxyethanol
substances.summary: A preservative commonly used in 'paraben-free' cosmetics and personal care products. Considered effective and, at typical cosmetic-use concentrations, lower-concern than some other preservatives -- but it is its own chemical with its own limits, not a neutral stand-in, and the same 'diversify rather than rely on one product long-term' logic that applies to parabens applies here too.
mitigation_tips: 'Paraben-free' describes what's absent, not what replaced it -- check the actual ingredient list if minimizing preservative exposure broadly is the goal, not just parabens specifically.
Rotate/diversify personal care brands rather than using one product exclusively long-term, the same habit that helps with parabens.
substances.pubmed_query: phenoxyethanol cosmetic preservative safety
substances.technical_note: Phenoxyethanol is metabolized primarily via hepatic alcohol/aldehyde dehydrogenase to phenoxyacetic acid and excreted in urine, without the estrogen-receptor activity that concerns researchers about parabens or bisphenols -- a genuinely different toxicological profile, not just a differently-named version of the same concern. A 2020 review (Nowak et al., Environmental Research) surveying paraben-alternative preservatives (phenoxyethanol, formaldehyde-releasers, triclosan, isothiazolinones) found each carries its own adverse-effect profile; none is a simple like-for-like safety upgrade.

The advice for parabens applies here too: vary your products instead of relying on one for years.

substances.name: Tobacco and vape smoke indoors
substances.summary: Smoke from cigarettes, cigars and hookah is a complex aerosol of fine particles and thousands of combustion products, including recognized carcinogens; e-cigarette aerosol carries nicotine, ultrafine particles and flavoring compounds, generally at lower but non-zero levels. A comparative-risk analysis of data from 192 countries attributed about 603,000 deaths in 2004 to second-hand smoke, and a 2024 meta-analysis of 97 studies found a pooled relative risk of lung cancer of 1.24 among never-smokers exposed to it, rising with duration and intensity. The US Surgeon General's 2006 report found no risk-free level of exposure and concluded that ventilation and air cleaning cannot eliminate it; keeping smoke out of indoor spaces is what fully protects the people inside.
common_sources: smoke drifting in from a neighbor's unit
residue on furniture, walls and fabrics
mitigation_tips: Make your home and car fully smoke- and vape-free, for visitors too. Smoking outdoors, away from doors and windows, removes most of the exposure for everyone else.
Fans, open windows and air purifiers reduce but do not remove secondhand smoke; the US Surgeon General found that only keeping smoke out fully protects the people inside.
If you smoke and want support to stop, free coaching is available in the US at 1-800-QUIT-NOW, and a clinician can talk through options that make quitting more likely to last.

substances.technical_note: Second-hand smoke is a mixture exposure: fine and ultrafine particles deposit deep in the airways (see particle deposition), while semi-volatile constituents sorb to indoor surfaces and re-emit later as 'thirdhand' residue, which is why smoke-free rules work where ventilation does not. In the 2024 never-smoker meta-analysis, risk rose with duration, intensity and pack-years, and the setting-specific estimates (home 1.20, workplace 1.38) show the same agent behaving consistently across exposure contexts, the pattern that supports a causal reading.
substances.summary_plain: Smoke from cigarettes, cigars, hookah and vapes fills indoor air with fine particles that everyone in the room breathes. People who never smoked but live or work around smoke get more lung cancer, and the US Surgeon General found no level without effects. Opening a window is not enough. Keeping your home and car smoke-free is what works.

substances.name: Alcoholic drinks (ethanol)
substances.summary: Ethanol in beer, wine and spirits is oxidized mainly in the liver to acetaldehyde; the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies ethanol in alcoholic beverages, and the acetaldehyde formed from it, as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1). A dose-response meta-analysis of 572 studies found clear dose-risk relationships for cancers of the oral cavity and pharynx, oesophagus, colorectum, larynx and female breast, and the Global Burden of Disease 2016 analysis found that the level of consumption minimising overall health loss was zero standard drinks per week, with alcohol the leading risk factor for death and disability among people aged 15 to 49 worldwide. Risk rises with amount, so drinking less lowers it at every level, and during pregnancy the advice is none at all.
mitigation_tips: Less is better at every level: a few alcohol-free days each week and smaller pours both lower the total.
Swap one regular drinking occasion for an alcohol-free option (sparkling water, alcohol-free beer, tea) and notice whether it sticks.
During pregnancy the advice is none at all. If cutting back is hard, a clinician can help, and in the US SAMHSA's free, confidential National Helpline is at 1-800-662-4357.

substances.technical_note: Ethanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase and CYP2E1 to acetaldehyde, then by ALDH2 to acetate. A common ALDH2 variant, frequent in East Asian populations, slows that second step, so acetaldehyde builds up (the flushing response) and the upper-digestive cancer risk per drink is higher: a clear example of how inherited differences in metabolic enzymes change the dose that actually reaches tissue.
substances.summary_plain: Alcohol in beer, wine and spirits is broken down in the liver into a compound that can damage cells. Large studies link drinking to several cancers, including mouth, throat, bowel and breast, and the risk grows with the amount. A global analysis found that the amount with the least health loss was zero. Drinking less helps at any level.

substances.name: Untested private well water
substances.summary: About 44 million people in the US drink from domestic wells, which fall outside the Safe Drinking Water Act, so testing and treatment are up to the owner. A US Geological Survey model estimated that about 2.1 million of them use wells with arsenic above 10 micrograms per liter, the federal limit for public systems, and nitrate from fertilizer and manure is common in agricultural areas: an updated review found the strongest evidence, beyond infant methemoglobinemia, for colorectal cancer, thyroid disease and neural tube defects, sometimes at levels below the regulatory limit. Bacteria from septic systems and runoff can also reach wells, especially after heavy rain. None of these can be seen or reliably tasted; a certified laboratory test is the only way to know, and treatment can then be matched to what is found.
common_sources: shallow wells near farms or septic systems
wells in regions with arsenic-bearing rock
mitigation_tips: Test your well at least once a year for bacteria and nitrate through a state-certified lab (your state or county health department can point you to one), and test for arsenic and other local concerns at least once.
Test again after flooding, a change in taste, smell or color, or any work on the well or septic system.
Match treatment to the result: choose a filter or system certified for the specific contaminant found, since no single filter removes everything.

substances.technical_note: Arsenic in groundwater is mostly inorganic arsenite and arsenate, efficiently absorbed from water and methylated in the liver; chronic exposure is associated with skin, bladder and lung cancer and with cardiovascular effects. Nitrate itself has low intrinsic toxicity, but under conditions that favour endogenous nitrosation it forms N-nitroso compounds, which is why the associations in the review depend on factors such as diet that affect nitrosation, and why a public-system limit set for infant methemoglobinemia may not capture every effect.
substances.summary_plain: About 44 million people in the US drink from home wells, which public water rules do not cover. Arsenic from rock and nitrate from farm runoff are common, and germs can get in after heavy rain. You cannot see or taste them. A test from a certified lab is the only way to know, and a filter can then be matched to what it finds.

substances.name: Carbon monoxide (CO)
substances.summary: An odourless, colourless gas from incomplete combustion: furnaces, water heaters, gas ranges, fireplaces, portable generators, fuel-burning space heaters and vehicles in attached garages. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin far more tightly than oxygen, so a room can reach harmful levels before anyone notices, and early symptoms (headache, dizziness, nausea) are easily mistaken for flu. CDC surveillance for 2005 to 2018 found about 3.3 unintentional deaths per million people each year in the US, most often in winter, with the highest emergency-visit rates in young children and the highest death rates in adults over 80; a 2023 analysis found accidental deaths rising from 2015 to 2021, with over half occurring at home. A working CO alarm near sleeping areas, yearly appliance checks, and never running engines or generators indoors are the standard protections.
mitigation_tips: Put a working CO alarm on every level of the home and near sleeping areas; test it monthly and replace it by the date printed on it.
Never run a generator, grill or engine indoors or in an attached garage, even with the door open, and keep generators well away from windows and doors.
Have fuel-burning appliances, flues and chimneys checked every year before the heating season.
If the alarm sounds, or several people feel unwell at once, get everyone outside into fresh air and call 911 or the fire department from there.

substances.technical_note: Carbon monoxide's affinity for haemoglobin is roughly 200 to 250 times that of oxygen, so carboxyhaemoglobin accumulates even at modest air concentrations and clears slowly on room air; it also binds myoglobin and cytochrome oxidase, which is why the heart and brain are most affected. The 2023 mortality analysis found no measurable effect of state laws requiring residential alarms, a reminder that a law is not the same as a working alarm in the right place.
substances.summary_plain: A gas you cannot see or smell, made when fuel burns: furnaces, water heaters, gas stoves, fireplaces, generators and cars in attached garages. Early signs feel like the flu: headache, dizziness, nausea. It happens most in winter. A working CO alarm near where you sleep, and never running a generator or engine indoors, are the simple protections.

substances.name: Dust, fumes and chemicals at work
substances.summary: Work is where many people meet the highest concentrations of anything in their day: mineral and wood dust, welding and metal fumes, solvents, pesticides, diesel exhaust and, in older buildings, asbestos. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 analyses attributed about 17% of the burden of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and 10% of asthma to airborne occupational exposures, and an estimated 349,000 cancer deaths in 2016 to 14 occupational carcinogens classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, led by asbestos, secondhand smoke at work, silica and diesel engine exhaust. In the US, employers must make safety data sheets available for hazardous chemicals, and the most effective protections remove or enclose the source, with ventilation next and respirators last.
mitigation_tips: Ask for the safety data sheets for the products you work with; US employers must make them available, and they list what each product contains and the protection it needs.
Favour controls that remove the exposure (a safer product, an enclosure, local exhaust ventilation) over relying on masks; if a respirator is needed, it should be fit-tested.
Keep work clothes and shoes out of the home and wash them separately, so dust does not come home with you.
If you have symptoms you connect to work, military service or a hobby, an occupational medicine clinician can help; US veterans can ask the VA about its toxic exposure screening.

substances.technical_note: Occupational exposure limits (OSHA PELs, NIOSH RELs, ACGIH TLVs) are set for healthy adult workers over an eight-hour day, and many OSHA limits date from the early 1970s, which is why the hierarchy of controls aims well below them rather than at them. Respirable crystalline silica and asbestos act through deposition of particles and fibres in the distal lung: the same particle-deposition physics as air pollution, at far higher doses.
substances.summary_plain: Work can bring the highest levels of dust, fumes or chemicals in your day: silica and wood dust, welding fumes, solvents, pesticides and diesel exhaust. Global studies link them to a real share of lung disease and some cancers. The best fixes remove or enclose the source, then add fresh air, with masks last. You can ask to see the safety sheet for what you work with.
